sections.h2: Selling a house in Evesham Township
sections.html:
Evesham Township is a large Burlington County suburb in South Jersey. Speed here depends on the fire department's resale certificate, a clean permit history and the state forms that travel with the deed.

Evesham spreads over roughly 29 square miles. Residents numbered 46,826 in 2020 and an estimated 49,525 in 2025, the largest head count of any Burlington County municipality. Many people say Marlton when they mean Evesham. Marlton is the best known community inside the township and shares ZIP code 08053 with much of it, so mention both in your listing.

A slice of Evesham lies in the Pinelands Area, a state zone with separate land use rules. Owners near the wooded edge should look at the zoning map first, because those rules can limit additions or new structures for the next owner.

sections.h2: Home values and who owns them
sections.html:
Most Evesham homes are lived in by their owners, and values sit above the national median (2020 to 2024 estimates).

About 89 percent of residents stayed put over the past year. Few homes come up for sale, so one that lingers gets noticed. A price near the township median lands in the higher state fee band described under closing costs.

sections.h2: Roads and transit buyers ask about
sections.html:
Route 70 and Route 73 define the township, and buyers judge a house by how it connects to them. Route 70 cuts east to west across the north of the township, Route 73 runs along the western border, and County Route 544 (Marlton Parkway and Taunton Lake Road) links the two. A grade-separated interchange replaced the old Marlton Circle in 2011, and commutes toward Philadelphia and Cherry Hill became more predictable.

  • NJ Transit bus route 406 runs through the township between Berlin and Philadelphia.
  • The Atco station, just across the border in Waterford Township, carries Atlantic City Line trains to Philadelphia 30th Street and the Atlantic City Rail Terminal.

Resale certificate requests go to the Evesham Township Fire Department. Its site, eveshamfire.org, posts inspection scheduling and fees. Start that request early so the paper is in hand by closing day.

Permits go through Community Development, Room 204 of the Township Building at 984 Tuckerton Road in Marlton. Hours are 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays. The construction office is at 856-983-2914, then option 4. A construction permit confirms that work meets fire and building codes, and an insurer can refuse a claim tied to work done without one.

  • A shed or fence needs a zoning permit. A fence around a pool also needs a building permit that meets the pool barrier code.
  • A homeowners association may need to approve a shed or fence first.
  • Interior sump pump or French drain work needs a construction permit, while exterior-only drainage work does not.
  • For flood zone questions, use the FEMA Flood Map Service Center or the township mapping portal.

Did an earlier owner finish a basement, build a deck or add a pool with no paperwork? Fix that before listing. Ask the construction office whether an inspection or a closed-out permit is needed, then keep the paperwork with your closing file. Buyer attorneys request permit history, and a gap can hold up a sale for weeks.

sections.h2: Selling a rental or short-term rental
sections.html:
A rental house can be sold, though its registration and fire inspection records need to be pulled together first. Short stays booked through Airbnb or Vrbo are treated like long-term leases. The house needs a fire department inspection and a registration with the Township Clerk's Office.

Every change of tenant triggers a compliance certificate covering smoke alarms, carbon monoxide alarms and a portable fire extinguisher (N.J.A.C. 5:70-2.3). Skipping it costs a $500 penalty. The fire department sets inspection fees.

With tenants in place, expect the buyer to ask for the lease, the deposit figure and the latest inspection certificate. A cash buyer who needs vacant possession should put that in writing before signing, which leaves time to plan notice periods. For landlord and tenant disputes, the township points people to the Burlington County courts and Legal Services of New Jersey.

Two items fall on the seller at closing: the state Realty Transfer Fee and a Gross Income Tax residency form. Both go to the Burlington County Clerk along with the deed. The Division of Taxation prices the fee per $500 of the deed price, and on sales over $350,000 the $200,000 to $550,000 band costs $4.80 per $500. That band covers a house priced near Evesham's median.

Sales above $1 million carry an extra graduated percent fee, also the seller's, that begins at 1 percent of the whole price. Few Evesham sales reach that level.

New Jersey residents generally sign the GIT/REP-3. A form dated October 1, 2025 or later has to be the current edition or recording is refused. The state GIT/REP Unit, 609-322-9275, answers form questions. Sellers who live out of state owe at least 2 percent of the price as an estimated payment unless an exemption applies.

The county clerk offers a free Property Fraud Alert service that alerts owners when a document is recorded under their name. Sign up before you sell and keep it after.

sections.h2: How a fast as-is sale moves
sections.html:
The order below assumes clear title and no open permits.

  • Collect your deed, latest tax bill, rental registration if any, and a mortgage payoff statement.
  • Ask the fire department for the resale certificate. Fix what it flags, or write into the contract who will.
  • Your closing attorney orders the title search and prepares the deed plus the fee and GIT/REP filings.
  • Close, hand over the keys, and the attorney records the deed at the county clerk.

A cash buyer may take the house as it stands. That ends repair haggling but not the certificate or the state filings. On older parcels the title search can surface easements or old liens, and the attorney must clear them before the deed records. Before committing, get the price, closing date and the party paying for each inspection in a single written offer.

faqs.q: Do I need a certificate from the township to sell my house in Evesham?
faqs.a: Yes. The Evesham Township Fire Department issues it for residential resales, and eveshamfire.org lists scheduling and fees. Book the inspection once you decide to sell.

faqs.q: What happens if work on my Evesham house was done without a permit?
faqs.a: The buyer's attorney will probably want it settled before closing, and an insurer may deny a claim tied to unpermitted work. The construction office, 856-983-2914 option 4, can explain what a retroactive permit takes.

faqs.q: Who pays the realty transfer fee in an Evesham sale?
faqs.a: You do, as the seller. It is collected at recording and tied to the deed price, with a further graduated fee above $1 million. The closing attorney or title company gives you the exact number.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house in Evesham if I live out of state?
faqs.a: Yes. You file a GIT/REP form and, unless an exemption on it applies, prepay at least 2 percent of the price as estimated Gross Income Tax. That payment counts against what you finally owe when you file.

faqs.q: Is part of Evesham in the Pinelands?
faqs.a: Yes, a portion. The township zoning map and Pinelands Commission maps show which lots are covered, so check your parcel before you market it.
